captions.instagram:
How does an umbrella work?

Push one sleeve up a stick and eight ribs swing out, bend like bows and pull a sheet of cloth drum tight. Open an umbrella in 3D, work its linkage, and see why the wind turns it inside out.

→ An umbrella is a folding roof: eight ribs, eight stretchers and one sliding runner under a sheet of cloth.
→ Each rib, its stretcher and the shaft make a triangle. Push the runner up and the triangle has to open.
→ Near the top the cloth pulls tight. The ribs bend like bows and the top spring holds the runner against them.
→ The cloth is cut a little small, so the ribs bend like bows. Cloth pulls, ribs push, and the roof goes stiff.
→ A 2 mm raindrop falls at about 6.5 metres a second. A 20 km/h breeze pushes it 40 degrees off straight down.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/umbrellaclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does an umbrella work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Push one sleeve up a stick and eight ribs swing out, bend like bows and pull a sheet of cloth drum tight. Open an umbrella in 3D, work its linkage, and see why the wind turns it inside out.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/umbrellaclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/umbrellaclear

In this video:
• A folding roof on a stick. An umbrella is a shaft, eight thin ribs hinged at the top, eight stretchers that hinge on one sliding runner, and a canopy sewn from eight cloth panels.
• One push opens eight ribs. Each rib, its stretcher and the shaft make a triangle.
• Cloth pulls, ribs push. The cloth is cut a little small.
• Rain slants, so tilt the shaft. A 2 mm raindrop falls at about 6.5 m/s, so a 20 km/h breeze pushes rain about 40 degrees off straight down.
• Why it turns inside out. Drag grows with the square of wind speed, and a cup catches nearly four times as much air as a dome.
• The one that fits in a bag. A pocket umbrella has a telescopic shaft and ribs in three hinged sections.
